for Evaluating Emotional States in Virtual Humans

emotional states, which are generated and rendered via morph target modifications.
ABSTRACT
The digital animation process is a complex endeavour requiring pro-
fessional animators to acquire substantial expertise and technique
through years of study and practice. Particularly, facial animation,
where virtual humans express specific mental states or emotions
with a desire for realism, is further complicated by the “Uncanny
Valley” phenomenon. In this context, it is posited that pre-validated
facial expressions for certain emotions could serve as references for
the novice or inexperienced animators during the facial animation
and posing process of their virtual humans using morph targets,
also known as blend shapes or shape keys. This research presents
a comparative study between two Facial Expression Recognition
(FER) systems that employ pre-trained models for facial recognition
applied to emotion recognition in virtual humans. Given that these
systems were not designed or trained for this particular purpose
but for facial recognition in real humans, this study aims to investi-
gate their level of applicability in scenarios where virtual humans
are used instead of real humans. This assessment is a critical step
towards evaluating the feasibility of integrating FER models as part
of a support tool for facial animation and the posing of virtual hu-
mans. Through this investigation, this research provides evidence
of the reliability of applying the FER library and Deepface systems
for emotion recognition in virtual humans, contributing to inves-
tigating new ways to enhance the digital animation process and
overcoming the inherent complexities of facial animation.

INTRODUCTION
The intricate orchestration of movement within three-dimensional
computer-generated entities, known as human-like “virtual hu-
mans” (both human characters and human-like figures), has in-
creasingly demonstrated its profound importance across various
application domains [2], [13]. In the entertainment industry, these
digital constructs are integral to generating stylized and photo-
realistic animated characters. Additionally, they serve as digital
surrogates for actual actors in scenes characterized by elevated
risk, logistical complexity, or those deemed currently unfeasible to
capture in the physical world, a technique frequently employed in
high-production-value digital cinema and AAA video games [22].
Beyond entertainment, these technologies find significant utility in
more analytically rigorous contexts, where they are harnessed to
simulate human facial and full-body kinematics for training, proce-
dure simulation, and various tasks necessitating recognition and
classification.
In modelling and animating digital avatars or virtual humans,
facial expressions assume a paramount role [1], serving as the linch-
pin for interpreting and recognising emotional states and potential
[13]. Consequently, facial expressions constitute a sophisticated


SVR ’23, November 06–09, 2023, Rio Grande, Brazil
Jonas de Araújo Luz Junior and Maria Andréia Formico Rodrigues
non-verbal communication medium, embodying an intricate array
of human sentiments and thought processes [8], [9]. Within virtual
human facial animation, the preeminent challenge hinges upon the
authentic portrayal of instantaneously discernible nuances in the
generated facial expressions. The goal is to ensure these expressions
are sufficiently lifelike, natural, and persuasive [18], [17]. Failing
to achieve this level of realism could inadvertently provoke the
disconcerting effect known as the “Uncanny Valley” [19]. However,
the psychological concept of “willing suspension of disbelief” [12]
allows readers, film viewers, and game players to embrace and em-
pathize with virtual humans, including their unrealistic animations,
within the medium’s stylistic universe.
The process of animating the facial expressions of virtual hu-
mans needs an initial preparation of the 3D geometric mesh of the
model. This task helps the animator implement the modifications
for each animation keyframe sequence. Among the techniques for
geometric mesh preparation, traditional methods include articulat-
ing the face via a digital skeleton, wherein the “bones” map onto
the mesh vertices—and using morph targets (also known as blend
shapes) [22]. These represent predefined modifications of individ-
ual facial regions or the entire facial geometric mesh, embodying a
certain expression. When artfully combined by the animator, these
shapes create a distinctive expression, typically associated with
a specific emotion intended for communication to the target au-
dience [18]. More contemporary techniques for facial animation,
which are becoming increasingly robust, are employed when the
utmost degree of realism is the objective. Some examples include
procedural muscle simulation, physics, and motion capture (mocap)
of live actors [2]. However, these advanced techniques demand
significant investment in both equipment and personnel.
Indeed, the effective and persuasive representation of facial ex-
pressions, embodying a diverse range of human emotions, demands
a degree of skill from the animator. This ensures that the expres-
sions crafted, via blend shapes, for instance, adequately depict the
intended emotions of the target audience. When considering more
conventional facial animation techniques through rigged meshes or
morph targets, with manual storyboard creation from keyframes, a
typical scenario for novice animators and game developers, mark-
ing these expressions becomes labour-intensive, monotonous, and
prone to errors [16]. Frequently, there arises a need for a “second
opinion” on the suitability of the synthesized expression concerning
the evoked emotion. In this context, it would be advantageous for
the animator to access a more agile mechanism that could expedite
the evaluation of the created expressions, even at a prototyping
stage, derived from blend shapes or rig bones, using, for instance,
known emotion groups.
This comparative analysis explores the applicability of Facial
Expression Recognition (FER) systems, established and tested on
real individuals, to support the validation or evaluation of 3D facial
expressions configured in virtual humans. The assessment includes
six emotional categories, along with a neutral state: anger, disgust,
fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise [10], [11]. Although FER sys-
tems were not originally designed to recognise facial expressions in
virtual humans [24], this work seeks to ascertain whether such sys-
tems could contribute to generating facial animations with diverse
types of emotions.
The comparative analysis conducted in this study was made
feasible following the rendering of facial images of numerous char-
acters, which were subsequently modified using specific morph
targets to represent the predetermined emotions. The resulting im-
ages were then submitted to the FER systems for evaluation. This
process aimed to ascertain these systems’ “hit” accuracy rate in
recognizing the pre-labelled emotions.
In brief, the main contributions of this work are the following:
• Expanding FER systems’ applicability to evaluate and vali-
date 3D facial expressions in virtual humans.
• Evaluating a comprehensive range of emotional states, in-
cluding six emotions and a neutral state, in the context of
virtual humans.
• Pioneering the use of FER systems for recognizing facial
expressions in virtual humans to facilitate diverse facial ani-
mations.
• Defining and implementing a new reproducible analysis pro-
cess involving the rendering and emotional modification of
multiple characters’ facial images.
• Offering insights into FER systems’ accuracy rate in recog-
nizing pre-labelled emotions in virtual humans.
After presenting a background summary of the facial expression
recognition systems, we delve into the specifics of two chosen
systems, the FER library [26] and Deepface [25]. Following, we
detail our evaluation methodology for using FER systems on virtual
human expressions, describing selected tools and implemented
scripts. We then present the procedure we defined and implemented
for the FER solutions evaluation. Finally, we perform a comparative
analysis of the solutions, present the results and limitations of our
study, and conclude with a final discussion and directions for future
work.
2
FACIAL EXPRESSION RECOGNITION
SYSTEMS
Facial Expression Recognition (FER) systems represent a subset
of artificial intelligence methodologies focused on discerning and
classifying human emotional states based on facial cues [26]. These
systems employ intricate machine learning algorithms to analyze
visual data, extracting distinctive facial features linked to various
emotional states. While the applications of FER systems span sev-
eral domains—from interactive entertainment to mental health
monitoring—they are primarily designed to interpret emotions in
real humans. The advent of FER systems has greatly contributed
to understanding non-verbal communication and its technological
implications [1].
In the field of Facial Expression Recognition (FER), there are sev-
eral prominent open-source libraries, including Deepface, EmoPy,
Py-FEAT, and RMN [24]. These systems have been developed to
analyze and interpret emotions from facial expressions using image
or video data, typically applying advanced machine learning tech-
niques [23], such as neural networks trained on extensive databases.
EmoPy focuses on recognising basic emotions from facial expres-
sions in images, leveraging convolutional neural networks. Py-
FEAT provides a holistic approach, offering tools for face detection,

landmarking, and emotion recognition. RMN uses robust and adap-
tive methods for face detection, featuring the integration of both
geometric and texture features.
Attending the requirements of this research, we focus on the
FER library [26] and the Deepface library [25]. The FER library [26]
was chosen for its straightforward implementation and ease of use,
as it provides a real-time facial emotion recognition system trained
on FER2013 dataset [15]. The FER library was primarily chosen for
its open-use philosophy. It is open-source and licensed under the
MIT license, allowing its integration into software with various
licensing modalities. The ease of implementation and use also made
the FER library a compelling choice for this research.
On the other hand, Deepface [25] is one of the most comprehen-
sive libraries available. It offers an extensive range of functionalities,
not limited to facial recognition, verification, and emotion analy-
sis. Deepface is designed to utilize deep learning models trained
on large-scale databases, thereby enabling high output accuracy.
Furthermore, being a “hybrid face recognition package”, Deepface
employs various face recognition models, with the VGG-Face model
[3] serving as its default.
3
METHODOLOGY
In this study, to enable the analysis of each FER system and its
potentialities for recognizing a set of emotions (anger, disgust, fear,
happiness, sadness, surprise, and a neutral state) in expressions
simulated in a virtual human, we first generated a database of
labelled facial images of virtual humans representing each of these
recognizable emotions. We created this dataset using Unity engine
[27], [7] by developing a plugin prototype for this game engine.
This prototype automated the activation of the facial blend shapes
and subsequent rendering of the faces of the generated models.
Following the creation of our previously labelled image database,
we submitted it in the batch form to two distinct FER systems—the
FER library [26] and the Deepface library [25], utilizing the Python
language [28]—for the assessment of the dominant emotion and
the degree of detection of the expected emotion in each image. The
findings were preserved in a Pandas DataFrame [21], which served
as the foundation for subsequent analyses.
To generate emotion-representative images on the faces of the
virtual humans, we chose to use the lineage of 3D character models
known as Genesis [5]—including Genesis, Genesis 2, Genesis 3,
Genesis 8/8.1, and Genesis 9 [4]. This selection was strategically
driven by the advanced capabilities of our licensed versions, which
come pre-equipped with distinct morph targets specifically tailored
for each recognizable emotion, thus offering a superior framework
for the task at hand. It is important to note that the predefined
emotions are linked to their specific morph targets, created and
defined by their animations and 3D artists. Therefore, the accuracy
of emotion labelling ultimately depends on the artists’ judgment.
While the interpretation of pre-existing morph targets for facial
emotions in these character models may be subject to the viewer’s
subjectivity, we posit that, given they were crafted to represent
specific emotions, these morph targets can serve as reliable mark-
ers for emotion labelling in this assessment. Moreover, being a
customizable character platform [5], the Genesis character models
allowed us to generate a representative diversity of virtual humans
regarding age, gender, ethnicity, and skin colour.
4
FACIAL IMAGES GENERATION PROCESS
The previously mentioned process we defined and used for ren-
dering the facial images depicting various emotions, which were
subsequently submitted to the two aforementioned FER systems,
begins with character generation. This involves creating diverse
3D characters varying in age, gender, race, and skin colour using
the Daz Studio software [4]. Each character is then transferred to a
game Unity project [27] using the Daz to Unity Bridge plugin [6].
Following this, if necessary, adjustments are done before placing
the characters within the 3D scene.
To orchestrate this process, we also developed an original proto-
type extension for the Unity editor which systematically:
(1) Locates and identifies 3D characters placed within
the
scene,
stemming
from
a
GameObject
named
CharacterCollection;
(2) Positions the FacialCameraRig (as shown in Figure 2), a
specially created object in the scene that maintains between
one to three cameras and a point light element, in front of the
character’s face. Subsequently, it renders – akin to “taking
a picture” – the character’s face in its neutral state. The
generated images, tagged with the emotion key “neutral”,
are then saved in a pre-determined folder;
(3) Each identified character undergoes facial modifications us-
ing previously known morph targets for each emotion. These
modifications are configured through the MappedMorph class
which is derived from Unity’s ScriptableObject class; and
(4) Utilizing the FacialCameraRig, images of the modified char-
acter face are captured for each character and morph target,
and subsequently saved in the predetermined folder.
The comprehensive process outlined above is performed in the
3D scene’s edit mode, thereby eliminating the need for actual scene
execution.
Additionally, in the phase outlined in step (4), each morph target
is activated at four progressive levels: 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%,
as depicted in Figure 3. By this method, we determine during the
subsequent analysis phase of the results obtained from the FER
system at which level the emotion designated by the morph target
will potentially be recognized. During the experimental process, we
configured the FacialCameraRig GameObject with three cameras,
all pointing towards the character’s face, located from the head
bone of the model’s skeletal rig, with one frontal and the other two
shifted to the left and right, respectively. The frontal camera also
has a point light component to illuminate the character’s face from
the front. Figure 2 shows the arrangement of the FacialCameraRig
in the scene.
Our analysis showed that while adding complexity, the side-
shifted cameras did not improve the FER systems’ facial recogni-
tion. Thus, we deactivated them and evaluated the tests using only
central camera images. The side-shifted cameras’ negligible contri-
bution to facial recognition was confirmed by the high failure rate
of recognition from their images, as demonstrated in Table 1, with
the number of instances where the system was unable (NA count)

Also, considering our study aims to assess the applicability of

FER SOLUTIONS EVALUATION
We submitted the rendered images from Unity to the FER systems
used in this evaluation through a Python Jupyter notebook [20]
that we wrote for this purpose, following the procedure outlined
below:
(1) The fundamental data of each character is read and extracted
from a spreadsheet file and loaded into a Pandas DataFrame
[21]. This file contains the names of the characters along

depicted in Table 2.
(2) The Unity-rendered images are read in batch from a prede-
fined directory. Each read image’s filename identifies the
“photographed” character, the selected emotion (morph tar-
get), its activation level (25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%), and the
camera’s relative position (left, center, or right). The image
filenames adhere to the following format:
<CharacterID>+<Emotion>+<Level>+<CamID>.png
These values become columns in the Pandas DataFrame that
will store the results, created in the previous step.
(3) The images are then batch submitted to two FER systems,
the FER library and Deepface, from which we retrieve the
following parameters: the predominant emotion identified
by the FER system, its detection level, and the detection level
of the originally labelled emotion. These obtained values also
feed into corresponding columns in the Pandas DataFrame
result.
(4) The correspondence (or lack thereof) between the labelled
emotion and the emotion detected by each FER system is
checked and attributed to the respective columns in the result
DataFrame, labelled as <FER System> - Hit.
Upon completion of this process, we obtain the result DataFrame,

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS AND RESULTS

are classified by us as “failures” of the FER systems. Consequently,
the FER systems’ accuracy, when their identified emotion matches
the labelled one, is presented in Tables 4 and 5.
The progressive improvement in the accuracy of both FER sys-
tems, as evidenced in Table 4, was anticipated. This is because a
low-activation morph target may inadequately represent the in-
tended emotion, even for human recognition, as shown in Figure 3.

it is “sculpted” or “modelled” into its final state (that is, 100% of
morph target application), with intermediary levels generated via

The neutral state, denoted as Morph Intensity at level zero
in Table 4 and explicitly indicated as the first Labeled Emotion
in Table 5, achieved an accuracy rate above 50%, in both evaluated
FER systems. Generally, the FER library outperformed the Deepface
(in its default configuration) in recognizing labelled emotions.
Assessing FER system accuracy by emotion, a noteworthy result
is that neither evaluated system recognized the labelled emotion
“disgust.” This observation prompted an investigation to discern if
“disgust” was identified by any of the studied systems. We found that
only the Deepface FER system identified “disgust” in a single image
of the character Genesis 9 Male #1, labelled with the emotion
“angry” and with its morph target applied at 100%, as shown in
Figure 5. Arguably, character emotion identification in this instance
may be ambiguous even for human visual interpretation.
Both Tables 4 and 5 show that, in total, the accuracy of Facial
Expression Recognition (FER) systems seldom exceeds 20%. Specif-
ically, the FER library correctly identified emotions in 19.8% (see
the Total value for column FER) of labelled cases, while Deepface
achieved this in merely 13.2% of images (see the Total value for
column Deepface).

image or did not recognize it at all in most cases, with 374 out of

correctly identified the labelled emotion. Individually, Deepface cor-

Further into the investigation, we aimed to pinpoint matching
pairs between labelled emotions and those identified by each FER
system, to discern potential FER system misinterpretations. Our
new findings are presented in Tables 7 and 8. These tables extend
the results shown in Table 5, providing a count of the non-matching
results to the labelled emotion and their relative percentage to the
total of each emotion.
The new tables reveal a clear pattern of high error rates in emo-
tion identification for the “neutral state” of the character across
all emotions in both FER systems, except for the identification of
the “happy” emotion by the FER library. To investigate this, we
constructed Table 9, which displays the number of identification
failures corresponding to the character’s neutral state. As the morph

7
LIMITATIONS
It is also important to acknowledge the limitations of our study.
As this was a novel exploration of FER usage for the authors, we
imposed certain restrictions to control the material used in the
study, such as:
(1) The virtual humans used in the emotion image production
were all created by the same manufacturer (Daz) [4], al-
though different model lineages were utilized. Similarly, the
native morph targets or blend shapes used belonged to these
characters, potentially resulting in more similarities than
differences. The labelled emotions are determined by blend
shapes and defined by animators and 3D artists. The accu-
racy of these labels is thus subject to the creators’ judgment,
which is appropriate given the context of virtual humans
lacking real emotions. Additionally, to minimize unrelated
interferences, the virtual humans were presented without
accessories such as hair, large beards, clothing, glasses, etc.
(2) The camera and lighting configurations used for image ren-
dering and the background were strictly controlled. At the
same time, the initial exploration of different camera angles
was conducted, some of which were discarded (see Table 1
and Figure 2), and variations in lighting or the utilization of
additional cameras to optimize recognition accuracy were
not explored.
(3) Among the various available FER solutions, we selected only
two, the FER library [26] and Deepface [25], both used in
their default configurations without exploring tool settings
to optimize image recognition and emotion accuracy.
The above restrictions, by promoting a certain degree of stan-
dardization of the input to this experiment, may have induced
biased results. Despite these limitations, our research aimed to shed
light on the potential applicability of FER systems in the context of
virtual humans and their facial expressions. By utilizing 3D char-
acters and evaluating them with FER library and Deepface, we
aimed to assess the accuracy and usefulness of these systems in the
modelling and production of virtual human expressions.
8
FINAL DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
This comparative study employed FER systems, traditionally used
for real human expression recognition, to identify expressions in
virtual humans — a task for which they were not initially designed.\nThis investigation aimed to assess the accuracy of these FER sys-\ntems in detecting virtual human expressions. The insights garnered\nfrom this research have the potential to stimulate exploration into\ninnovative solutions for modelling and generating realistic emo-\ntional expressions in virtual human models.\nConsidering the previously presented limitations, our investiga-\ntion revealed that the FER systems displayed a low level of facial\nemotion recognition in virtual humans for the selected character\nset and under defined testing conditions. In most images processed\n(374 images of 500, 74.8%), the evaluated FER systems could not\nidentify faces or their expressions. On a broader scale, even when\naccounting for cases with emotion morph target activation at an\nintensity of 75% or higher, along with the neutral state, the emotion\nrecognition rate achieved by the tested FER systems did not surpass\nthe overall hit percentage of 30% associated with the FER library.\nWe conclude that applying FER systems (initially designed for\nreal human face recognition) for emotion recognition in virtual\nhumans has low reliability. Thus, we suggest adapting the ma-\nchine learning models used for human FER to virtual humans to\naddress this challenge as a future research direction. It might also\nbe valuable to have real individuals review the emotion labelling of\nvirtual humans before training. Finally, employing Explainable AI\n(XAI) techniques [14] to comprehend model-driven emotion selec-\ntion could be explored within the application context, potentially\nserving as an auxiliary tool for animators. Such efforts would be\nbeneficial for developing a support tool for facial animation.
